video_title: MacroVoices #552 David Rosenberg: Navigating The Noise
gist: David Rosenberg argues the energy shock won't become lasting inflation because it isn't feeding into wages, and that housing, rents and Chinese competition are disinflationary. He blames the bond selloff mostly on a hawkish Fed regime change under Warsh and debt-funded hyperscaler capex, and sees the Nov 3 midterm gridlock and Nov 4 Treasury refunding as overlooked bond-bullish catalysts (he owns 2-year notes and is adding gold). The trade desk segment flags weak equity breadth, 10-year yields above 5.3%, a strong dollar, and an S&P put hedge.

themes.theme: Energy shock is not secular inflation without wages

insights.claim: David Rosenberg argues the consensus inflation scare is overstated: the same pundits warning about energy/diesel-driven inflation in 2026 wrongly predicted a tariff-driven inflation surge in 2025.
insights.speaker: David Rosenberg
insights.so_what: Fade the inflation-alarmist consensus; prior shock (tariffs) failed to produce persistent inflation.
insights.quote: is inflation the big threat that it's made out to be? In my opinion, it's not.

insights.claim: Core goods CPI, where tariff pass-through should have shown up most, decelerated from about 1.5% year-over-year a year ago to below 0.7% now, a 4-year low, despite the biggest effective tariff rate increase since the early-to-mid 1930s.
insights.speaker: David Rosenberg
insights.so_what: Tariff costs were absorbed by exporters, importers or margins rather than passed to consumers.
insights.quote: Today, it's running below 0.7%. It's at a 4-year low.

insights.claim: Rosenberg expects energy prices to stay elevated rather than collapse, but because inflation is a rate of change, merely peaking prices is enough to stop the inflation momentum as the shock falls out of year-over-year data.
insights.speaker: David Rosenberg
insights.so_what: Inflation prints should roll over even without an energy price collapse.
insights.quote: But remember that inflation is not a level. Inflation is a rate of change.

insights.claim: Unlike Gulf War I in 1990, when WTI went from $20 to $40 and quickly reversed, Rosenberg expects no rapid reversal this time: refined product prices will stay elevated but not rise continuously.
insights.speaker: David Rosenberg
insights.so_what: Don't count on an energy-price collapse for disinflation; count on base effects.

insights.claim: Despite the ongoing US-Iran conflict, traffic through the Strait of Hormuz has recovered to the highest since the war began, and Gulf exports are ramping, notably via Saudi Arabia's east-west pipeline.
insights.speaker: David Rosenberg
insights.so_what: Physical supply normalization argues energy prices are peaking.

insights.claim: The host argues refinery destruction is a stickier inflation risk than crude, because destroyed refineries take years to rebuild, leaving plenty of crude but scarce diesel.
insights.speaker: Host
insights.so_what: Crack spreads/diesel may stay elevated longer than crude prices.

insights.claim: Rosenberg's core framework: a price shock becomes sustained inflation only if it feeds into wages; otherwise it produces negative real wages, negative real demand and downward pressure on the other ~80-85% of the price basket, especially discretionary goods and services.
insights.speaker: David Rosenberg
insights.so_what: Watch wages, not oil, to judge whether inflation becomes persistent.
insights.quote: Prices have to feed into wages because if the price shock doesn't feed into wages, it hits the wall in the labor market

insights.claim: The 2021-2023 inflation lasted about 18 months because it fed into wages, driven by roughly $2 trillion of stimulus checks and paying people not to work, which forced businesses to pay up to attract labor; the 1970s spiral relied on unionization and COLA clauses that don't exist today.
insights.speaker: David Rosenberg
insights.so_what: Today's labor market lacks the bargaining power that enabled past wage-price spirals.

insights.claim: An energy price shock without wage catch-up is economically akin to a tax increase: it drains purchasing power rather than creating self-reinforcing inflation.
insights.speaker: David Rosenberg
insights.so_what: Treat the energy shock as growth-negative, not inflation-persistent.
insights.quote: It's really akin to a tax increase.

insights.claim: Labor is about 30% of costs at the retail level, making it roughly six times more powerful than energy for inflation, yet markets watch energy tickers because labor costs aren't visible minute by minute.
insights.speaker: David Rosenberg
insights.so_what: Investors are over-weighting the visible but less important inflation input.

insights.claim: Rosenberg will only change his view on inflation when he sees escalating collective bargaining agreements and wage trends, naming average hourly earnings in non-farm payrolls as the most important number to watch.
insights.speaker: David Rosenberg
insights.so_what: Average hourly earnings is the key trigger for the bond-bull vs inflation debate.

insights.claim: NY Fed President John Williams said in a September 29 speech that there is no evidence the price shocks are entering wages, so inflation is unlikely to become self-reinforcing, implicitly pushing back on Fed Chair Kevin Warsh.
insights.speaker: David Rosenberg
insights.so_what: Signals potential internal Fed dissent against the hawkish chair.

insights.claim: Today's labor market differs from the post-COVID one: quits, hiring and job openings rates are not surging, and nominal wages are decelerating.
insights.speaker: David Rosenberg
insights.so_what: No wage-price spiral precondition exists.

themes.theme: Bond yields driven by Fed regime change under Warsh

insights.claim: Rosenberg says the rise in the 10-year yield is about 90% real rates and only 10% inflation expectations.
insights.speaker: David Rosenberg
insights.so_what: The bond selloff is about policy/capital demand, not inflation fears.

insights.claim: Three of the four biggest hyperscalers are now net free-cash-flow negative and are borrowing in long-dated bond markets across multiple currencies to fund AI capex, so corporate credit demand now competes with government borrowing and pushes up real rates.
insights.speaker: David Rosenberg
insights.so_what: AI capex has shifted from cash-funded to debt-funded, a new source of term-rate pressure.
insights.quote: three of the biggest of the four are now net free cash flow negative.

insights.claim: Rosenberg dismisses the $40 trillion debt narrative: the 10-year yield was below 4% in February when debt was $39 trillion, after a trillion was added from October 2025 to February 2026 with no market reaction.
insights.speaker: David Rosenberg
insights.so_what: Debt levels didn't change; don't attribute the yield spike to fiscal fears.

insights.claim: The biggest change behind higher yields is 'regime change at the Fed': Rosenberg believes most of the rise would not be happening if Powell were still chair; the 10-year was about 4.4% when Warsh took over in June and is up about 90 bps since.
insights.speaker: David Rosenberg
insights.so_what: Yields are a Fed-expectations story that can reverse if expectations reset.
insights.quote: What's changed the most is we have regime change at the Fed.

insights.claim: Rosenberg criticizes Warsh for focusing on headline rather than core inflation and on the share of PCE components rising faster than 3%, a metric that weighs a bag of peanuts the same as an automobile.
insights.speaker: David Rosenberg
insights.so_what: The Fed's new reaction function is noisy and hawkish-biased.
insights.quote: A bag of peanuts to Kevin Morris is equivalent to an automobile.

insights.claim: When applying for the job, Warsh favored the Dallas Fed trimmed mean inflation measure, last around 2.3%, only 30 bps above target, but he no longer references it.
insights.speaker: David Rosenberg
insights.so_what: Underlying inflation is near target; Warsh's hawkishness is a stance, not a data need.

insights.claim: Market pricing swung from one or two rate cuts in February to a Fed hike at the last meeting and now three or four more tightenings priced, which explains well over 100 bps of the rise across the Treasury curve.
insights.speaker: David Rosenberg
insights.so_what: If the Fed doesn't deliver the priced hikes, front-end and belly yields have room to fall.

insights.claim: Historical pattern: rookie Fed chairs typically hike at their first opportunity (e.g., Greenspan in 1987, Yellen in December 2015); the last to cut at a first meeting was Arthur Burns in 1970 as a recession began.
insights.speaker: David Rosenberg
insights.so_what: Warsh's early hawkishness fits a pattern of credibility-flexing, not necessarily a sustained hiking cycle.

insights.claim: Warsh has not unveiled a framework and leaves the market guessing, so markets read every syllable as hawkish; the 10-year yield rises six or seven bps whenever he speaks.
insights.speaker: David Rosenberg
insights.so_what: Poor Fed communication is inflating term premium, which could unwind.

insights.claim: Shorting bonds is crowded and fashionable: Rosenberg cites near-record net speculative short positions in 10-year note futures on the CBOT.
insights.speaker: David Rosenberg
insights.so_what: Crowded short positioning sets up a potential short-covering bond rally.
insights.quote: It is sexy and fashionable to hate the bond market right now.

insights.claim: Rosenberg owns a lot of two-year notes because he doesn't believe the Fed will hike four times, noting the Fed didn't even signal that.
insights.speaker: David Rosenberg
insights.so_what: Front-end Treasuries offer asymmetric upside if hikes are priced out.

insights.claim: Rosenberg compares the bond market to stocks in January 2009 or summer 1982: terrible performance, underowned, heavy shorts and disdain, signs of capitulation that create a buying opportunity.
insights.speaker: David Rosenberg
insights.so_what: Contrarian long-duration entry point for patient investors.

themes.theme: Midterm gridlock and Nov 4 refunding as bond catalysts

insights.claim: Historically, when one-party control swings to divided government after a national election, about 80% of the time the economy slows, inflation falls, and bond yields fall over the following two years.
insights.speaker: David Rosenberg
insights.so_what: Divided government after November 3 is a bullish setup for bonds.
insights.quote: 80% of the time the economy slows. 80% of the time inflation goes down. And 80% of the time bond yields go down

insights.claim: Rosenberg expects Democrats to take the House on November 3, with prediction markets showing over a 50% chance they take the Senate, ending six years of fiscal stimulus via gridlock.
insights.speaker: David Rosenberg
insights.so_what: Fiscal drag from 2027 onward; incrementally negative for aggregate demand.
insights.quote: there's no more fiscal stimulus in the economy after November the 3rd.

insights.claim: The One Big Beautiful Bill delivered one-off stimulus this year through depreciation allowances and large income tax refunds that can't be extrapolated; the economy was also supported by the high-end equity wealth effect and AI spending, partly offset by imports.
insights.speaker: David Rosenberg
insights.so_what: 2026 growth was flattered by non-repeating fiscal one-offs.

insights.claim: Treasury's November 4 quarterly refunding announcement is an overlooked catalyst: Rosenberg expects Treasury Secretary Bessent may cut long-dated issuance in favor of bills, as Yellen did in November 2023, which helped trigger a ~100 bp 10-year rally from late October to end of December.
insights.speaker: David Rosenberg
insights.so_what: Shift to bill issuance could flatten term premium and spark a long-end rally.
insights.quote: November 4th is a Treasury Footing announcement.

insights.claim: Rosenberg says Treasury's ~$6 billion bond buybacks are a drop in the bucket against a market turning over about $1 trillion daily; Treasury's real power is in choosing issuance maturities.
insights.speaker: David Rosenberg
insights.so_what: Watch issuance mix, not buybacks.

insights.claim: Market history: one-party sweeps (Trump 2016, Republican red wave 2024, Clinton 1992) drove stock surges and bond selloffs, while shifts to split government (e.g., the 1994 Gingrich Contract with America) produced major bond rallies.
insights.speaker: David Rosenberg
insights.so_what: Political regime shifts systematically move bonds.

insights.claim: The host finds it puzzling that stocks sit near all-time highs with low volatility a month before midterms that may hand Congress to the party that twice impeached the president.
insights.speaker: Host
insights.so_what: Political risk appears underpriced in equity volatility.

insights.claim: Rosenberg calls the administration's policy incoherent: an affordability push ahead of the midterms alongside a trade war with Canada, and a proposed $5,000 dividend to voters (about $1 trillion) if Republicans keep Congress, which he says would be inflationary like the 2020-2022 stimulus checks.
insights.speaker: David Rosenberg
insights.so_what: Policy unpredictability adds noise; giveaways would be the real inflation risk.

themes.theme: Hidden disinflation: housing, rents, China AI

insights.claim: Housing is in recession: new home inventory is about 8.5 months of supply despite heavy builder discounting, and new home prices are down 8-12% year-over-year.
insights.speaker: David Rosenberg
insights.so_what: Housing is a deflationary force the market ignores.
insights.quote: Housing h housing is in a recession.

insights.claim: The US multifamily market is hugely overbuilt because construction was planned on demographic assumptions that no longer hold given zero population growth from out-migration, keeping rents deflating.
insights.speaker: David Rosenberg
insights.so_what: Shelter disinflation should persist.

insights.claim: Plugging real-time rents and home prices into CPI would put headline near zero and core well below 2%; with lags, shelter, which matters far more than energy in CPI, should pull inflation down.
insights.speaker: David Rosenberg
insights.so_what: Lagged shelter disinflation is a coming tailwind for bonds.

insights.claim: At Jackson Hole, Warsh mentioned AI eight times and housing only once, which Rosenberg sees as evidence the Fed is ignoring housing weakness.
insights.speaker: David Rosenberg
insights.so_what: The Fed may be blind to a key disinflationary sector.
insights.quote: he mentioned AI eight times. He mentioned housing once.

insights.claim: Citing Matt Barry, the host raises the risk that free Chinese open-source AI models, nearly as good as frontier models from a few months ago and runnable on in-house hardware that air-gaps data, could lead corporations to abandon OpenAI and Anthropic.
insights.speaker: Host
insights.so_what: A potential pin to the AI bubble via commoditization of frontier models.

insights.claim: Rosenberg says there are no real barriers to entry in AI and expects China to again act as a source of global disinflation, offsetting AI-driven inflation in memory chips and semiconductors, before even counting future productivity gains.
insights.speaker: David Rosenberg
insights.so_what: AI competition is ultimately disinflationary, supporting bonds.

themes.theme: Equity breadth weakness beneath mega-cap indices

insights.claim: The average and median US stock is down about 15% from its 52-week high while 50% of S&P 500 market cap sits in 20 stocks; rate-sensitive areas like regional banks, homebuilders, retailers, restaurants, hotels, cruise lines, theme parks and small caps are in correction.
insights.speaker: David Rosenberg
insights.so_what: Fed tightening is already biting; index strength masks broad damage.
insights.quote: nobody talks about the fact that the average and median stock in the United States is down 15% from the 52- week highs.

insights.claim: The median S&P 500 stock is 16% off its 52-week high and only 20% of S&P 500 stocks are above their 50-day moving average, with the equal-weight index and Russell 2000 breaking down while the cap-weighted index holds near highs.
insights.speaker: Patrick (trade desk host)
insights.so_what: Breadth divergence signals fragility under the mega-caps.

insights.claim: A drop of just about 150 S&P points could push the index into a sell zone with a gamma flip, rising implied volatility hitting vol-targeting funds and CTA sell triggers that could generate tens of billions of dollars of selling.
insights.speaker: Patrick (trade desk host)
insights.so_what: Systematic flows create a nonlinear downside trigger close to current levels.

insights.claim: Trade idea: with the S&P 500 near 7,653, buy the January 14, 2027 7,430 put (about 3% OTM, ~30 delta, ~136 points, under 2% of notional, breakeven near 7,300) as a hedge through earnings, two Fed meetings, the midterms and Hormuz developments, since 3-month volatility is near the bottom of its one-year range.
insights.speaker: Patrick (trade desk host)
insights.so_what: Cheap vol plus a catalyst-heavy Q4 favors owning downside protection.

insights.claim: CFTC positioning: large speculators in Nasdaq futures jumped from the 80th to the 100th percentile in one week (57th a month ago), driven mostly by short covering (~12,000 contracts) plus ~8,000 new longs, the most bullish net positioning since 2017, versus the 36th percentile for S&P and 7th for the Russell.
insights.speaker: Patrick (trade desk host)
insights.so_what: Extreme Nasdaq long positioning raises contrarian reversal risk.

themes.theme: Rates, dollar, oil and gold cross-asset stress

insights.claim: The trade desk reports the 10-year Treasury yield trading above 5.30% and the 30-year above 5.60%, levels unseen in decades, with an accelerating rate of selling despite a softer-than-expected inflation report that only helped the short end.
insights.speaker: Patrick (trade desk host)
insights.so_what: Long-end stress persists independent of inflation data; a policy catalyst is needed.

insights.claim: The US dollar index hit 52-week highs as the euro broke to 52-week lows below 1.13, driven by widening rate differentials and Europe's disproportionate terms-of-trade hit from the Hormuz disruption; the euro could fall to 1.10 or 1.08.
insights.speaker: Patrick (trade desk host)
insights.so_what: Dollar strength may signal global funding stress.

insights.claim: Crude oil, which traded above $100 in mid-September, has retraced about 50% of its advance to the low $90s and is range-bound awaiting a catalyst on a peace deal or Hormuz flows, with political incentives to keep it stable before the midterms.
insights.speaker: Patrick (trade desk host)
insights.so_what: Oil is consistent with Rosenberg's 'peaking energy' view.

insights.claim: Rosenberg sees gold in a corrective phase within an intact secular bull market, hurt this year by rising real rates and a weak dollar turning strong; he cut gold in his model portfolio earlier this year and began adding again during the correction.
insights.speaker: David Rosenberg
insights.so_what: Buy gold weakness; the secular driver is unchanged.

insights.claim: The gold bull market's fundamental driver is central bank reserve reallocation from dollars into gold: gold's share of central bank FX reserves fell from 70% in 1980 to 10% in 1999 and is now about 30%, so mean reversion is incomplete.
insights.speaker: David Rosenberg
insights.so_what: Gold bull ends only when central banks stop diversifying, which hasn't happened.
insights.quote: We haven't even undertaken the full mean reversion trade yet.

insights.claim: Gold broke below the $4,200 area and could retest $4,000 or wash out to about $3,800; it needs to sustain above $4,500 to turn the technical trend bullish, and is expected to be range-bound into the elections.
insights.speaker: Patrick (trade desk host)
insights.so_what: Near-term gold levels: support 4,000/3,800, bullish pivot above 4,500.
